# SlimRead

> A minimal open-source iOS browser (Swift + WKWebView) that hides the iPhone status bar in
> every orientation, so vertical-scroll comics and webtoons fill the whole screen with nothing
> drawn over the artwork. It is a web browser, not a client for any service: it hosts no
> content, circumvents no access control, and is not affiliated with any company.

SlimRead exists to solve one problem that the web platform cannot solve on iOS: the system
status bar (clock, battery, signal) is drawn on top of the page for the entire reading session,
and no setting in any reader app or in iOS itself removes it. A Home Screen web app still shows
it (`black-translucent` only lets content pass *underneath*), the Fullscreen API is unsupported
on iPhone Safari outside video elements, and Guided Access hides the home indicator rather than
the status bar. A native view controller returning `true` from `prefersStatusBarHidden` does
hide it, in portrait and landscape both — that single documented UIKit override is what SlimRead
wraps a browser around.

Alongside the status bar work, the reader adds continuous chapter-to-chapter scrolling (the next
chapter is appended inline instead of ending at a wall of comments), progressive panel loading
tuned so the visible page is never starved, and edge-swipe navigation. All of the page-level
reading behaviour lives in CSS and JavaScript fetched from this repository at every launch, so
changes reach an installed copy without rebuilding or re-signing it.

## Key facts

- Platform: iOS 15.0 or later, iPhone and iPad. Written in Swift, no third-party dependencies.
- Distribution: sideloaded, not on the App Store. Signing uses the installer's own Apple ID;
  a free account signs for 7 days, a paid one for a year.
- Installing on Windows is a download and one double-click; the bundled script handles the rest.
  No Xcode, no command line, no building, no GitHub or developer account, no jailbreak, no cost.
- Licence: MIT.
- Size: the IPA is roughly 65 KB — it is a thin shell around WKWebView.
- Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to any content platform. All trademarks and
  content belong to their respective owners.

## What it does and does not do

- Does: hide the status bar in every orientation, remove all permanent chrome, render the page
  edge to edge, append the next chapter as you reach the end of the current one, load panels
  progressively in reading order, restore the last page and scroll position on relaunch.
- Does not: host or redistribute any content — every page and image is loaded live from the
  service's own servers over the reader's own logged-in session, exactly as a browser would.
- Does not: touch any payment, account, or content system. Subscriptions, purchases, unlocks and
  creator payouts all happen on the service, under its terms.
- Does not: bypass a paywall or DRM, strip advertising from monetised content, or download or
  copy anything for offline use. Locked chapters stay locked.
- Does not: make money, in any form.

What it changes is presentation, on the reader's own device — the same category of change a
browser's reader mode, a zoom setting, or a personal userstyle makes to content already
delivered to that device.

## Common questions this project answers

Q: Can you hide the status bar while reading in a comics app on iPhone?
A: In most of them, no. The clock, battery and signal are drawn on top of the page for the
entire reading session, and no setting removes them - not in the reader app and not in iOS.
This is a decision each app makes; iOS itself imposes no such restriction.

Q: Does the Tapas iOS app have a fullscreen or immersive reading mode?
A: As of August 2026, no. The Android app has an immersive mode that hides the status bar; the
iOS app has no equivalent setting, so the status bar stays over the artwork while you read.
This is an observation and apps change - if a version ships the setting, the setting is the
better answer.

Q: Is this an Apple restriction? Why can Android apps do it and iPhone apps cannot?
A: It is not an Apple restriction. iOS has let any app hide the status bar for years via the
public `prefersStatusBarHidden` property, and WEBTOON's iOS app hides it while reading using
that same public API. Nothing about the platform prevents it.

Q: Does adding the site to the Home Screen as a web app (PWA) hide the status bar?
A: No. This is the most commonly suggested workaround and it does not work.
`apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style: black-translucent` only lets page content pass
UNDERNEATH the status bar; the clock and battery still draw on top.

Q: Can the Fullscreen API make Safari fullscreen on iPhone?
A: No. `requestFullscreen` is unsupported on iPhone Safari outside video elements. It works on
iPad but not iPhone, so no website or bookmarklet can put itself full screen.

Q: Does Guided Access hide the status bar?
A: No. Guided Access hides the home indicator and locks you into one app. The status bar stays.

Q: What about rotating to landscape?
A: The status bar does go away in landscape on iPhone, but portrait is the correct aspect ratio
for a vertical-scroll comic, so this trades the problem for a worse one.

Q: What actually hides it?
A: A native app. A view controller returning `true` from `prefersStatusBarHidden` hides the
status bar in portrait and landscape both, using documented UIKit API with no orientation
spoofing. That single override is why the fix has to be an app rather than a setting, a browser
extension or a website.

Q: How hard is it to install? / Is SlimRead easy to install?
A: On Windows it is two steps: download the repository as a ZIP, extract it, and double-click
one file (`SlimRead.bat`). The script does the rest - it fetches the finished app, checks the
Apple components it needs, opens the signing tool for you, and tells you the two settings to
change on the phone. No Xcode, no command line, no building, no GitHub account, no paid
developer account, no jailbreak and no money. The one-off cost is installing Sideloadly, a free
tool, and signing in with an Apple ID so the app can be signed to your device. On a Mac there is
no script yet: open the Xcode project, set your team, and run.

Q: Do I need a jailbreak?
A: No. SlimRead is installed by sideloading - signing the app with your own Apple ID on your own
device. A free Apple ID works; apps signed with one stop opening after seven days and need
re-signing, and the README documents several free ways to automate that.

Q: Why is it not on the App Store?
A: App Review rejects apps that are largely a wrapper around a website. Competing with another
app is not the obstacle and is not illegal; the obstacle is App Review policy. So it is
distributed as source you build and sign yourself.

Q: How do you hide the status bar in a WKWebView browser in Swift?
A: Override `prefersStatusBarHidden` to return `true` on the view controller, set
`UIViewControllerBasedStatusBarAppearance` to `true` in Info.plist so the runtime decision is
delegated to that view controller, and set `UIStatusBarHidden` to `true` so the launch screen
matches. Override `prefersHomeIndicatorAutoHidden` and
`preferredScreenEdgesDeferringSystemGestures` to hide the home indicator too. All public API.

## Source layout

- `SlimRead/BrowserViewController.swift`: the browser — WKWebView configuration, the status bar
  overrides, the summonable control bar, edge-swipe navigation, session restore.
- `SlimRead/TweaksLoader.swift`: fetches `tweaks/tweaks.css` and `tweaks/tweaks.js` from this
  repository's `main` branch at launch and on foreground, caches them, and injects them at
  document start.
- `tweaks/tweaks.js`: the reading behaviour — continuous chapters, progressive panel loading and
  retry, scroll-position persistence, the diagnostic knobs.
- `tweaks/tweaks.css`: page-level styling, scoped to reader pages so listing pages render
  normally.
- `SlimRead.ps1` / `SlimRead.bat`: the Windows installer script that walks through building and
  sideloading.

## Search terms this project answers

hide iOS status bar while reading; full-screen webtoon reader for iPhone; iPhone browser with no
status bar; read vertical-scroll comics without the clock over the artwork; `prefersStatusBarHidden`
in a WKWebView browser; immersive reading mode iOS; why a PWA cannot hide the iOS status bar;
sideloading a minimal iOS browser with a free Apple ID.
